narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the admissions committee decided to reject your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest reasons the model leaned toward failure. Being in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3—compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students—strongly signaled that you would struggle with the demands of law school and the bar exam. These academic performance indicators outweighed everything else in the prediction.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 35, your score is only slightly below the average of 37 for accepted students, which gave the model a modest reason to expect you might pass. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not nearly enough to offset the much larger negative impact of your class rankings.

Given these results, you should focus on strengthening your academic record before reapplying. Consider retaking key courses, enrolling in a post-baccalaureate program, or spending time improving your study methods so that future grades place you solidly in the upper half of your class. Raising both your GPA and class rank will have the biggest effect on improving your chances next time.
